scope: All 30 principles linked from English homepage; original operational synthesis, not copied article text

principles.title: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
principles.symptoms: Polished screen is praised while task failures persist; users overestimate ease from surface aesthetics.
principles.mechanism: Positive first impression biases perceived usability and can conceal operational friction.
interventions: Keep visual polish consistent but test real task completion
Separate beauty/perception ratings from observed success and errors
Correct affordance, legibility and flow before decorative refinement
principles.misapplications: Do not treat attractive screenshots or preference ratings as proof a task is usable.
principles.verification: Unmoderated first-task completion and observed misclicks improve, not just appearance scores.

principles.title: Choice Overload
principles.symptoms: Users hesitate at a large option set; abandon comparisons or repeatedly switch choices.
principles.mechanism: Comparison effort grows with undifferentiated alternatives and weak decision support.
interventions: Group by user goal and explain distinguishing attributes
Offer trustworthy filters, search or side-by-side comparisons
Preselect only defensible defaults and show all material tradeoffs
principles.misapplications: Do not hide legitimate alternatives or manufacture a preferred choice.
principles.verification: Find-rate, decision time, regret or backtracking and choice quality with representative users.

principles.title: Chunking
principles.symptoms: Dense walls of text, undifferentiated settings, long identification strings.
principles.mechanism: Semantic grouping allows recognition and efficient scanning without maintaining every item separately.
interventions: Cluster by meaning, not arbitrary item counts
Create clear headings, whitespace and progressive sections
Keep dependent information and actions together
principles.misapplications: Overfragmenting a task into many pages or meaningless cards introduces navigation cost.
principles.verification: Users can locate target facts and explain group boundaries without rereading.

principles.title: Cognitive Bias
principles.symptoms: Framing, defaults or misleading emphasis steer decisions; design critique assumes its own answer.
principles.mechanism: Mental shortcuts simplify judgments but can distort perception, recall and choices.
interventions: Inspect framing, defaults, anchoring and confirmation bias
Surface neutral comparisons and reversibility
Test alternative explanations and affected user groups
principles.misapplications: Do not exploit biases for coercive conversion or equate any user preference with bias.
principles.verification: Users can accurately explain options, costs, consequences, and opt out.

principles.title: Cognitive Load
principles.symptoms: Users reread, forget context, make preventable mistakes or struggle with irrelevant material.
principles.mechanism: Intrinsic task demands compete for limited cognitive resources with avoidable interface demands.
interventions: Reduce extraneous content, decisions and recall
Externalize state, rules, prior entries and next actions
Use familiar conventions and compact contextual help
principles.misapplications: Simplifying visually while hiding needed details increases load; learning effort is not always wasted effort.
principles.verification: Fewer context switches, fewer memory-dependent errors and comparable or better task outcomes.

principles.title: Doherty Threshold
principles.symptoms: After an action there is a dead period with no acknowledgement; interaction feels laggy.
principles.mechanism: Fast reciprocal system feedback preserves attention and the continuity of the task.
interventions: Acknowledge actions promptly and make pending work observable
Use skeletons or progress only when informative
Measure interaction latency and optimize critical path
principles.misapplications: 400 ms is a design heuristic, not a universal SLA; fake delays or false progress undermine trust.
principles.verification: Interaction-to-feedback and completion timing measured at slow devices/networks; no double submission.

principles.title: Fitts’s Law
principles.symptoms: Mis-taps, tiny icons, crowded toolbar controls or distant primary actions.
principles.mechanism: Target acquisition cost depends on both target size and distance.
interventions: Increase hit areas and separation without misleading visual bounds
Locate task actions near their context and within reach
Provide accessible keyboard and pointer alternatives
principles.misapplications: Do not replace user testing with a fixed pixel rule; large targets must not overlap or steal events.
principles.verification: Target misactivation and time improve for touch, mouse and motor-diverse participants.

principles.title: Flow
principles.symptoms: Users are repeatedly interrupted by modal prompts, latency or unclear goal state.
principles.mechanism: Engagement can emerge when task challenge matches skill and feedback stays intelligible.
interventions: Remove needless interruptions and keep task state stable
Offer graduated complexity and expert shortcuts
Give immediate meaningful feedback and a clear next action
principles.misapplications: Do not confuse time-on-site, addictive patterns or unbroken activity with useful flow.
principles.verification: Goal completion, uninterrupted task segments and user-reported sense of control improve.

principles.title: Goal-Gradient Effect
principles.symptoms: Users drop out near the end of a multi-step task and cannot tell how much remains.
principles.mechanism: Perceived proximity to an achievable goal can increase motivation.
interventions: Show honest progress with completed and remaining work
Shorten and stabilize the endgame
Provide save/resume and make completion criteria explicit
principles.misapplications: Never fabricate progress, move goalposts, or create manipulative urgency.
principles.verification: Completion and re-entry rates improve without inaccurate progress estimates.

principles.title: Hick’s Law
principles.symptoms: Main action competes with many equally weighted options; time-critical decisions drag.
principles.mechanism: Searching and choosing among non-obvious alternatives increases response time.
interventions: Prioritize relevant options by user intent
Group/sequence complex decisions while preserving comparison
Prefer a visible recommended path when its basis is clear
principles.misapplications: Do not remove needed expert choices, hide alternatives or assume fewer options always means faster expert performance.
principles.verification: Decision time, misselection and task completion compared by expertise and task criticality.

principles.title: Jakob’s Law
principles.symptoms: Common control behaves unexpectedly or familiar navigation is reinvented.
principles.mechanism: Users carry expectations from prior products into new ones.
interventions: Follow platform and category conventions for common tasks
Reserve novelty for distinctive user value
Offer migration cues or transition support for changed patterns
principles.misapplications: Do not fossilize harmful conventions; novel concepts can be justified with evidence.
principles.verification: First-use success and discoverability improve without prior instruction.

principles.title: Law of Common Region
principles.symptoms: Related items appear disconnected or unrelated elements share a box.
principles.mechanism: Perceived visual containment communicates grouping.
interventions: Use subtle shared surfaces or borders for meaningful groups
Remove containers that add no information
Ensure group titles and keyboard order match visual grouping
principles.misapplications: Too many bordered cards erode hierarchy and may fragment reading.
principles.verification: Users identify grouping and ownership correctly while scanning.

principles.title: Law of Proximity
principles.symptoms: Labels appear to belong to the wrong field or commands are visually detached.
principles.mechanism: Nearby items are assumed related.
interventions: Tighten spacing within groups and widen between groups
Associate help/error text with the correct control
Check responsive and zoom layout grouping
principles.misapplications: Proximity alone does not establish semantics for assistive technologies.
principles.verification: Visual and screen-reader associations match; no group confusion on small viewports.

principles.title: Law of Prägnanz
principles.symptoms: Complex silhouettes, decorative visual clusters or icons are difficult to parse.
principles.mechanism: Perception favors simple, stable interpretations of ambiguous visual structures.
interventions: Prefer unambiguous icon silhouettes and grouping
Limit competing shapes and nested ornamentation
Use labels for uncertain representations
principles.misapplications: Do not equate minimalism with meaning; simplicity may hide necessary distinctions.
principles.verification: Recognition and interpretation accuracy in brief exposure tests.

principles.title: Law of Similarity
principles.symptoms: Clickable elements look like plain text or unrelated controls share a misleading style.
principles.mechanism: Similar shape, color and size imply related meaning and behavior.
interventions: Give same role the same treatment across the app
Differentiate links, buttons, destructive actions and states
Support meaning with text and non-color cues
principles.misapplications: Visual similarity must not override underlying semantics or clear focus indication.
principles.verification: Users correctly predict control roles; no mistaken clickable text.

principles.title: Law of Uniform Connectedness
principles.symptoms: A sequence or group relationship is invisible despite physical separation.
principles.mechanism: Lines, frames and connecting surfaces provide strong grouping cues.
interventions: Connect steps and related fields visually when relationship matters
Use connectors only for real dependence or sequence
Preserve connection meaning under reflow and mobile
principles.misapplications: Connectors imply causality; do not draw them decoratively between unrelated data.
principles.verification: Users can identify membership and sequence at glance.

principles.title: Mental Model
principles.symptoms: Labels, controls or state transitions contradict how users expect the product to operate.
principles.mechanism: People use compact predictive representations built from experience.
interventions: Map users’ terms and expected object relationships
Match behavior to familiar analogies when warranted
Observe first-use expectations and correct model mismatches
principles.misapplications: Internal architecture and team jargon are not reliable proxies for user concepts.
principles.verification: Predict-then-use testing: expected destination, state and effect align with actual.

principles.title: Miller’s Law
principles.symptoms: Users must memorize labels or state across distant steps.
principles.mechanism: Limited working-memory capacity favors external memory and meaningful grouping.
interventions: Show prior context instead of making users remember
Chunk information by semantics
Add summaries and comparisons where recall is needed
principles.misapplications: 7±2 is not a universal cap on menu items, fields, cards or options.
principles.verification: Recall-dependent errors and user memory effort decrease.

principles.title: Occam’s Razor
principles.symptoms: Superfluous chrome, unnecessary flows, excessive abstraction or proliferating controls.
principles.mechanism: Between similarly capable alternatives, fewer unfounded assumptions and elements reduce burden.
interventions: Start from user goal and remove steps without losing capability
Make complexity prove its value
Review drafts by subtraction and empirical task coverage
principles.misapplications: The simplest-looking design is not always simplest to use; do not remove necessary information.
principles.verification: Core tasks remain complete and comprehensible with fewer steps or distractions.

principles.title: Paradox of the Active User
principles.symptoms: Long tours are skipped and first actions cannot happen until tutorial completion.
principles.mechanism: Newcomers usually act on their immediate goal instead of studying instructions first.
interventions: Enable a useful first action immediately
Place help where decisions occur
Provide progressive practice, starter templates and persistent revisit points
principles.misapplications: Critical safety, permission or consent requirements still need upfront clarity.
principles.verification: First-value time, help discoverability and novice error recovery improve.

principles.title: Pareto Principle
principles.symptoms: Team polishes low-frequency UI while top journeys contain persistent blockers.
principles.mechanism: Impact and usage are often unevenly distributed.
interventions: Identify high-value user goals and high-cost failures
Prioritize issues by user harm, frequency and importance
Include low-frequency high-risk cases explicitly
principles.misapplications: 80/20 is not a guaranteed distribution or grounds for excluding minorities or safety-critical tasks.
principles.verification: Top user journeys and high-severity cases show measurable improvement.

principles.title: Parkinson’s Law
principles.symptoms: Forms or flows take the whole available session despite low intrinsic effort.
principles.mechanism: Work tends to expand into time made available; ambiguity encourages wandering.
interventions: Use autofill, defaults and concise task paths
Show realistic scope and completion points
Reduce redundant entry and waiting
principles.misapplications: Do not impose countdowns or artificial pressure where careful judgment matters.
principles.verification: Task time falls without added errors, abandonment or stress.

principles.title: Peak-End Rule
principles.symptoms: Users remember anxious failures, confusing submission, or anticlimactic completion.
principles.mechanism: Emotional high points and the ending disproportionately influence remembered experience.
interventions: Map anxiety and delight across user journey
Make critical errors recoverable and high-stakes steps understandable
End with clear confirmation, next steps and truthful reassurance
principles.misapplications: A charming finish cannot justify an exploitative or broken core journey.
principles.verification: Completion confidence, recall, trust and recovery ratings improve.

principles.title: Postel’s Law
principles.symptoms: Input rejects harmless formatting differences; inconsistent error messaging after a near-correct entry.
principles.mechanism: Human input is variable and robust systems can normalize permitted variation.
interventions: Accept benign spacing/case/format variants at the UI boundary
Normalize deterministically and disclose canonical result when material
Validate strictly for security, meaning and irreversible actions
principles.misapplications: Never accept ambiguous monetary/security inputs, unsafe payloads or silently change user intent.
principles.verification: Permitted variants succeed; invalid cases receive specific guidance; no security regression.

principles.title: Selective Attention
principles.symptoms: Critical actions vanish in banner-like regions or multiple simultaneous updates compete.
principles.mechanism: Users filter stimuli according to task relevance and often miss unrelated changes.
interventions: Anchor essential actions near the active task
Avoid ad-like treatment for critical content
Make state changes perceivable without excess motion
principles.misapplications: Attention cues must not become distracting, deceptive or inaccessible.
principles.verification: Users notice key feedback and next actions during realistic multitasking.

principles.title: Serial Position Effect
principles.symptoms: Users forget important options hidden in long ordered lists.
principles.mechanism: First and last items can have memory advantage under some conditions.
interventions: Use semantic ordering and task priority first
Put high-importance anchors at predictable edges when appropriate
Verify search and scanning rather than relying only on order
principles.misapplications: Never reorder stable data or manipulate ranking solely to exploit primacy/recency.
principles.verification: Findability and recall measured across list lengths and user expertise.

principles.title: Tesler’s Law
principles.symptoms: Complex domain rules spill into forms and leave users to compute or translate requirements.
principles.mechanism: Inherent process complexity must be managed somewhere: user, system or organizational workflow.
interventions: Move deterministic repetition and validation into the system
Provide defaults and derived values with inspection and correction
Expose complexity only at the level needed for accurate decisions
principles.misapplications: Hidden automated assumptions can introduce uncorrectable errors; transparent complexity is sometimes essential.
principles.verification: Correct task completion improves with less manual effort and preserved user control.

principles.title: Von Restorff Effect
principles.symptoms: Everything is highlighted, or high-priority action blends into uniform surroundings.
principles.mechanism: An item distinct from otherwise similar peers is more likely to be noticed.
interventions: Reserve distinct treatment for the one important action or state
Use non-color cues and ensure contrast
Test whether emphasis aligns with user importance
principles.misapplications: If many elements compete for emphasis none stands out; do not design fake urgency.
principles.verification: Key action detection and error-state recognition improve for varied vision abilities.

principles.title: Working Memory
principles.symptoms: User must recall values from previous screen, compare distant items, or retain hidden state.
principles.mechanism: Temporary memory has limited capacity and decays during interruptions.
interventions: Keep query, selection and progress visible
Use review summaries and compare views
Preserve drafts and continuity across navigation
principles.misapplications: Do not force memorization as a substitute for exposing system state.
principles.verification: After interruption, users resume correctly without searching prior screens.

principles.title: Zeigarnik Effect
principles.symptoms: In-progress work disappears or users are uncertain whether to return.
principles.mechanism: Incomplete goals can remain cognitively salient, particularly when clearly represented.
interventions: Make unfinished tasks and resume actions visible
Persist work and show genuine remaining steps
Let users explicitly dismiss or abandon tasks
principles.misapplications: Do not deliberately leave loops unfinished or use guilt-based notifications.
principles.verification: Users reliably resume, finish or discard work on their terms.
